# SetProvenance

Namespace `Nfty.Core.Output` in assembly `Nfty.Core`.

```csharp
public static class SetProvenance
```

Whether the CookBook in front of you is the one a Set on disk was cooked from, and what to say when it is not.

**Why it matters.** `Generator` walks a recipe's `layerOrder` and consumes one weighted draw per layer, so moving a layer moves *which draw reaches it*. The same seed over a reordered — or otherwise edited — book therefore rolls different variants and different colors: not a re-render of the same collection, a different collection. Extending a Set with a book that did not cook it silently interleaves two generations under one set of token ids, and nothing else in the output records that it happened. `set.json`'s `cookbookSha256` is the only thread tying a Set back to its source archive, so it is what this compares.

**A warning, never a refusal.** Deliberately re-cooking an edited book is a legitimate thing to want; the author is the one who knows. And the text lives here rather than in a front-end for the same reason the reports in `Stats/` do — the CLI and a GUI should say the identical thing, not something similar.

## Methods

### IsSameBook(string?, string?) { #m-issamebook-system-string-system-string }

```csharp
public static bool IsSameBook(string? recordedSha256, string? cookbookSha256);
```

Whether a CookBook is the one a Set was cooked from.

**Parameters**

- `recordedSha256` (`string?`) - What the Set recorded at cook time.
- `cookbookSha256` (`string?`) - The hash of a CookBook on disk.

**Returns.** True when the two hashes are the same.

**Remarks**

Case-insensitive: both sides are written lowercase by `ArchiveIo.HashFile`, but `set.json` is plain JSON a person can edit, and an uppercase copy of the same hash is the same hash. Ordinal-ignore-case, not the current culture's, because a hex digit must compare the same under every locale.

A null on either side is FALSE here rather than "cannot tell", which is the opposite of what [`SetProvenance.Warning()`](Nfty.Core.Output.SetProvenance.md#m-warning-system-string-system-string) does with one - and deliberately so. Warning is asked "should I interrupt?", where silence is the honest answer to an unanswerable question; this is asked "is this the book?", where an unanswerable question is not a yes.

### Warning(string?, string?) { #m-warning-system-string-system-string }

```csharp
public static string? Warning(string? recordedSha256, string? cookbookSha256);
```

The warning to show before extending, or null when there is nothing to warn about.

**Parameters**

- `recordedSha256` (`string?`) - What the Set recorded at cook time — [`SetManifest.CookbookSha256`](Nfty.Core.Output.SetManifest.md#p-cookbooksha256), as `SetWriter.ReadExisting` reports it. Null when the Set predates the field, has no readable `set.json`, or was cooked from a book that never came from a file.
- `cookbookSha256` (`string?`) - The hash of the CookBook about to be used — `LoadedCookBook.SourceSha256`. Null for an in-memory book that never came from a file.

**Returns.** The warning text, or null when the two agree or cannot be compared.

**Remarks**

**A null on either side means "cannot tell", which is not "they differ".** Both sides are legitimately absent — an unsaved book has no file to hash, and a Set can be cooked from one — so warning on a null would fire on the ordinary case and train the author to ignore the one message that matters. Silence is the honest answer to a question that was not asked.
